title: Read a host's messages off a byte stream

blocks.text: A new acquirer link goes into pilot. Its interface spec says: "Every message is preceded by its length in two bytes, binary, most significant byte first. The length does not include the two length bytes. When the link is idle the host sends a message of length zero."

Our reader for that link, `FrameReader` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/FrameReader.java`, was never finished: its three methods are marked `TODO`. The comment on each says what it is for. Finish them so that `next()` returns each message the host meant, exactly as the host sent it, whatever the network does to the bytes on the way, and fails loudly when the connection drops in the middle of a message.
About 14 lines in total. The tests feed the reader streams that behave like real connections: some hand out a few bytes per read, some deliver several messages at once.

cases.says: a framed message comes back as exactly the bytes the host sent, without its length
a message longer than 255 bytes uses both length bytes and comes back whole
a message whose bytes arrive over several reads is still returned whole, because one read is not one message
two messages that arrive in one read come out one per call, each with exactly its announced length
the binary length is an unsigned number, so a length byte above 127 still counts up
a stream that ends before the announced length has arrived raises EOFException instead of returning a short message
a zero-length frame is a keep-alive and is skipped, so the next real message is returned

origin.section: 3.2 One Read Is Not One Message

concepts: The channel decides where a message ends and the packager what is inside it; a 2-byte binary length is an unsigned number, high byte first, and a wrong frame shows up as silence.
A receiver reads exactly the announced length, across as many reads as it takes and one frame per call, and a stream that ends early is an error.
